title: go-sdk streaming migration guide and idiomatic cancellation examples
creator: Miguel Santos
description: Produce a migration guide and a set of idiomatic Go examples for the Redwood Go SDK streaming API. Primary objective is to help application engineers migrate from the legacy ReadStream/StreamSession surface to the newer StreamIterator + ContextWrap helpers, with clear cancellation, timeout, and retry patterns and runnable example programs.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A markdown migration guide published to the SDK docs site covering the 3 most common migration patterns (simple forward-only streams, resumable partial-aggregation streams, and long-polling sessions). 2) Three standalone Go example programs checked into github.com/redwood-inference/go-sdk/examples/streaming/ that demonstrate: context cancellation with timeouts, client-initiated pause/resume, and coordinated per-message deadlines. 3) Unit + integration tests exercising the context-wrapper types and showing deterministic cancellation behavior in CI. 4) Design reviewed by two SDK engineers and a PM.
design_notes: We will avoid introducing new blocking APIs on the public SDK surface. Instead we provide two thin helpers: ContextWrap(stream) which ensures the SDK honors caller context cancellation immediately, and DeadlineSpan(ctx, perMessage time.Duration) which simplifies per-message deadline calculations. Chose a cooperative backoff of 50ms initial jittered up to 1s for resumable reconnects to avoid tight CPU loops seen in legacy examples. Rationale: teach users safer patterns rather than exposing advanced lease machinery in docs. Consider follow-up doc for advanced lease + checkpointing patterns.
test_plan: Unit tests: mock server that delays first token 500ms and ensure TimeoutWrapper causes Next() to return with ErrCanceled. Integration: run examples against local shim server in CI matrix with small and large latency to validate backoff jitter. Add deterministic timers (fake clocks) for flaky timing. Add a smoke test that runs examples/streaming/* and asserts exit code 0 within 10s under normal conditions.
